component.name: COSMIC Calculator
component.summary: Scientific calculator for the COSMIC desktop

description.p: A native scientific calculator for the COSMIC desktop, written in Rust with no runtime dependency on another language.

ul.li: IEEE 754 double precision, displayed to 15 significant digits
Stateful entry: only the equals key evaluates the expression
Automatic scientific layout in a landscape window
Follows the COSMIC theme, and inherits the accent colour from KDE, GNOME and XFCE
Decimal separator taken from the system locale
Live number properties: prime, harshad, palindrome, square, triangular, fibonacci

A side panel gives back exactly the width it took, so the keypad is the same size after closing one as it was before opening it. A panel is a fixed width and stays drawn at it, so width a drag of the window edge takes comes off the calculator column and width it adds goes to the calculator column — dragging in to the floor with a panel open used to charge every pixel of the drag to the panel, and closing it then handed back less than the panel was really holding and the keypad sprang wider than the window it had been resized in. The same bookkeeping decides the width the window opens at next time, which had been recording a calculator wider than the one on screen

The memory register starts off. Nothing is stored at startup, so the row under the display opened given over to the word "Memory:"; "Show memory contents" in the settings panel puts it back. MC, MR, M+ and M− work whether or not the register is on screen

app_bg's alpha channel means the same thing every other colour's does: 00 is invisible whatever colour it is written in, FF is the colour exactly as configured, and the values between are that colour as tinted glass over whatever is behind the window. The window background is the one colour the renderer does not blend — it is what the surface is cleared to, and a compositor reads those pixels as premultiplied — so #FFFFFF00 had been painting an opaque white window and #28313300 a tinted one, with only #00000000 coming out transparent

The palettes are one table in config.toml, each under its own id: [themes.RedmondLight], [themes.HighContrastDark.number]. The file used to repeat [[themes]] nineteen times with an id inside each entry and a bare [themes.number] under it, so nothing below the top of a palette said which palette it belonged to. A file written by an earlier version still loads, with everything tuned in it intact, and the next save rewrites it in the new shape
button_border_thickness is button_border_percent, which is what the value is — a percentage of the button's height. The old name is still read, so a hand-tuned file keeps its borders

Every colour off disk is checked rather than interpreted: a #, then hex digits and nothing else, and exactly six or eight of them. FF0000FF without the hash, #FF00 a digit short, #FF00GG with a character that is not hex — each is replaced by the shipped colour for that slot alone, and the colours either side of it in the same row still come out of the file
HighContrast Dark and HighContrast Light are High Contrast Dark and High Contrast Light. The id the file keys them by is unchanged, so nothing in an existing config.toml has to move

The theme picker is a scrolling list of one palette per row, in the same box and at the same height as the font family list, and it opens at the palette in force with the ones either side of it on screen. Nineteen names wrapped across the panel as buttons took a third of its height and had to be read across and down

± flips a minus already in front of the operand rather than wrapping a second one inside it. 5−3 is 5+3, since taking away a negative three is adding three, and −4 is 4, the sign coming off a number with nothing to subtract from — the same wherever a value begins, so sin(−3 is sin(3 and 2⁻³ is 2³. An operand after a +, ×, ÷ or a caret is still wrapped as (-x), and one already wrapped still unwraps

Every palette is written into config.toml in full — the name on its button in the settings panel, the three surfaces, the two text colours, the accent, the border thickness and the nine colours of each button group — and the file is what the window is painted with. A palette can be retuned by hand, or renamed, without rebuilding; the shipped tables are only where a fresh file starts from

Nothing in that section has to be right. A colour that is not #RRGGBB or #RRGGBBAA, a border thickness that is not a number in range, a whole button group written as one string: each falls back to the shipped value on its own rather than costing you every other setting in the file. A palette named twice keeps its first entry, one this build does not have is ignored, and one the file leaves out is put back. Only id is fixed, since that is how the rest of the app names a palette

A palette's name is stripped of control characters and of the invisible codepoints that let text render as something other than what it says, and is capped at 32 characters, before it reaches the button that carries it

Five more button groups a theme can paint on their own: percent, 1/x, rand, the two brackets, and the twelve trigonometric functions. Each one ships painted exactly as the group it was split out of, so nothing on screen moves until a theme says otherwise
High Contrast Dark and High Contrast Light are HighContrast Dark and HighContrast Light

Opening the history panel grows the window from its left edge instead of pushing the calculator sideways: the right edge stays put and so does every key under the pointer. The settings panel already behaved this way, by docking into the width added on its own side. A display server that will not tell a window where it is or let it move itself — Wayland does neither — still grows the window rightwards as before
config.toml records the version that wrote it, so a later release can tell what it is reading before it changes anything
The random-decimals caption in the settings panel drops its "(max 14)". The slider's own end already says where the limit is, and the limit moves with the upper bound as you type it

A bracket you open at the head of an exponent closes the exponent when you close it, the way a ) with no bracket of yours to close already did. 𝑒ˣ, (, 2, ), % is (e^(2))% — a hundredth of e² — where the percent was left up in the exponent as e^(2)%, which is e to the one-fiftieth. ! reads the same way, and a second caret raises the whole power rather than adding a level to it: 2, xʸ, (, 3, ), xʸ, 2 is (2³)² and not 2⁹. Every key that opens an exponent is covered — xʸ, 10ˣ, 2ˣ, 𝑒ˣ and EE

The base slot yˣ opens finishes the same way. 5, yˣ, (, 2, ), 7 is (2)⁵×7, where the 7 landed between the base and its caret and took the slot for itself as (2)×7⁵; a caret there now raises the whole power. The operators and the postfixes always managed it, so this is the digits and the carets catching up with them
The five inverse-function domain messages are punctuated like every other named case: Undefined: sin⁻¹(x) must be between −1 and 1, where the colon was missing on those five alone

The Cosmic palette sits after High Contrast Light in the settings list, with the twelve newer palettes after it. It is still the palette a fresh install starts on, and still the one an unreadable theme name in config.toml falls back to
Auto is called System on the decimal separator, the thousands separator and the corner radius — the choice that is not a choice, where the separators take the region's and the radius the desktop's

Button shape is Button corner radius, and offers 50%, 25% and 0% rather than names. That is what the keypad draws: the radius is a fraction of the button's own height, so a 50% key is a pill at every window size where a fixed pixel count would stop being round as the buttons grew. What config.toml records is unchanged, so a file an older build wrote still loads
The font list opens at the family in force, with the families either side of it on screen to compare against, rather than at the top of an alphabetical list of every family on the machine
Cupertino Dark and Cyberpunk wear a button border. Every other palette leaves it off, and a palette that asks for one gets at least a whole pixel of it however thin the setting

A negative exponent can be keyed at all: 2, xʸ, −, 3 is 2⁻³ and 5, EE, −, 3 is 5×10⁻³, with the sign drawn up in the slot the digits are going into. The press used to read as a change of mind about the operator, take the caret back and leave 2-, so there was no way to reach a negative exponent from the keypad

yˣ lifts the sign with the number it raises: −, 2, yˣ, 9 is 9⁻², where the sign was left on the line as -9² — the negative of nine squared, a different number. A minus that has something to subtract from is still a subtraction, so 5-2 then yˣ then 3 is 5-3²

A power whose slot a ) has closed is a finished value, and everything keyed after it says so. A digit starts a new factor — 2, xʸ, 3, ), 5 is 2³×5 where it used to run onto the end of the exponent and give 2 to the thirty-fifth — a postfix applies to the whole power as (2³)!, and a second caret raises the power rather than adding a level to it
! and % after a yˣ apply to the whole power too: 5, yˣ, 9, ! is (9⁵)!, the way 8^5-8 subtracts from the whole 8⁵. It used to read back as 9 raised to 5!

The five inverse-function error messages wear their −1 raised, the way the display writes those functions everywhere else: Undefined sin⁻¹(x) must be between −1 and 1. Flat, it read as a sin with a 1 subtracted from it

The memory register under the display is called Memory: rather than a bare M, with a no-break space before the value so the two are never split across lines. When it and the number-property labels would meet — a narrow window, or fifteen digits stored — it drops to a line of its own under them instead of being drawn over the fibonacci at the end of the row

The ASCII expression writes the decimal separator the settings are set to instead of always a dot, on screen and on the clipboard alike. The tokenizer reads either, so it is still text this calculator takes back

History rows are stored as the display writes them — √(9)×2𝑒, not the sqrt(9)*2*e the clipboard spells the same thing with — so a pasted expression keeps the characters that were pasted. Reading a row back is the clipboard's own paste pipeline, allow-list and length cap and all, so a hand-edited config.toml can put nothing into the buffer that the clipboard could not: a row that does not survive it is dropped whole and in silence, and is gone from the file on the next write

A font weight selector under the family, offering only the faces that family actually ships and following it as it changes. A weight the new family has no face for is drawn in the nearest it does have while the choice stays stored, so going back to a family that has it gets it again

Show angle mode and memory buttons hides the row above the keypad — the DEG/RAD switch and MC/MR/M+/M- — and gives the height it was taking to the expression display. Show memory is now Show memory contents

Every row of option buttons in the settings panel fills the panel's width, sharing it out in proportion to the names on the line, so a choice between two ends at the same edge as a choice between four rather than trailing off in the middle

Every colour a theme draws with is written down rather than worked out. A button group carries a fill, a label colour and a border colour for each of its three states — resting, hovered, pressed. The hover shade used to be an HSV lift of the base and the pressed shade a 10 percent darkening of it, with one label colour for the whole theme however little contrast it had against the key it landed on

AC/C and backspace have a colour group of their own so a theme can mark the two keys that take something away, and the display — the caption, the readout and the properties and memory under them — is a surface of its own that a theme can set apart from the window. Every shipped theme paints both exactly as before

Buttons can carry a border, off by default. The thickness is a percentage of the button's height rather than a pixel count, so an outline keeps its proportion as the window grows and a settings row does not wear the same line as a keypad key three times its size; the width rounds to a whole pixel so the line stays crisp, and it is drawn inside the button, so turning one on never moves anything
The alpha channel is live everywhere a colour goes: a button filled with 00000000 shows the background through it and is drawn by its border alone
The switches and sliders in the settings panel take the theme's own accent colour, which for the Cosmic palette is the desktop's

The Cosmic palette stops deriving anything: it takes the running desktop's own component colours — base, hover, pressed, the text on them and their border — so the keys hover the way the rest of the desktop hovers and an accent-coloured key wears the accent's own text colour, which is where its contrast used to go
Twelve new palettes: Texas, Tokyo, Cyberpunk, Plastic, Crystal, Barbie, Touch Light, Touch Dark, Emerald Light, Emerald Dark, Flat Orange Dark and Flat Green Light

The Custom palette is gone, and with it the copy of every colour config.toml carried so it could be hand-edited — that would be a hundred-odd colours in the file now. The file records which palette is on, and a name this build does not know falls back to the default rather than failing the load and taking every other setting with it

) closes what a key opened rather than bracketing round it. An exponent typed straight after the caret is a slot the display draws brackets round, and ) is how you say you are done with it: 2, xʸ, 3, ) is 2³ with the brackets down, where it used to write a pair round the whole power and give (2^3). The base slot yˣ opens closes the same way, stepping the cursor out past the power, so 5, yˣ, 6, ), + reads 6⁵+

A bracket closed inside a call's slot finishes that slot. 8, ʸ√x, (, 2, ), +, 2 reads root(8,(2))+2 — the sum lands outside the call, where it used to be carried up into the degree as root(8,(2)+2). Same for a logᵧ base

The base slot yˣ opens wears the placeholder brackets every other slot does, once it holds something and not only while it is empty: 5, yˣ, 6 reads (6)⁵, because that 6 is still the slot the next digit joins. A bracket you opened there yourself is real and stays after you close it
) with an operator still waiting for its right operand takes the operator back rather than closing over it: (5+ then ) is (5)
( keyed after a base that is already typed multiplies the power instead of landing in the slot: 5, yˣ, 6, ( is 6⁵×() where it was 6×()⁵, with the 6 pushed out of the slot it had just been typed into

− where a value begins is that value's sign rather than a subtraction: −, 6 is -6, not the 0-6 a supplied left operand made of it. +, × and ÷ still start an empty display on a 0, which is what they need and a sign does not

Every slot of logᵧ and ʸ√x takes a minus, so a negative base, degree, argument or radicand can be keyed at all — the press used to be dropped. And the two calls close over the sign along with the number: −, 4, logᵧ, 8, ) is log₈(-4), where the sign was left outside as -log₈(4), which negates the logarithm instead of taking one of a negative number
A decimal separator with no digits behind it goes when you move on from it: 5, ., + is 5+. Backspace is the one press that leaves it, since deleting it is what you are asking for

% and ! write themselves and nothing else — neither puts brackets round what it applies to any more. Keyed in an exponent they stay in the exponent, which is how the text reads them anyway: 2, xʸ, 5, % is 2^5%
The expression above the display comes down as soon as you add to the result under it. It is the expression that produced that result, so an operator or a digit keyed after = makes it no longer true

Every expression with no value now says which part of it has none, instead of a bare Undefined: a negative number under an even root or to a fractional power, a negative or a zero inside a logarithm, a logarithm base of 1, 0 or a negative, 0 to the zeroth or a negative power, division by 0, a zeroth root, the tangent and cotangent poles in either angle mode, the hyperbolic cotangent at zero, and the five inverse domains, which name the interval the argument has to be in. 0 raised to a negative power used to report Overflow, which said the answer was too big rather than that there is none

The thousands separator groups with a no-break space, and the readout no longer wraps. A grouped number that came a hair over the width the font was fitted to used to break at a group boundary into a line the display has no room for, so 1 234 567 read as 1 — which is a good deal worse than no grouping at all

The memory register sits under the display, at the size and in the colours of the number-property labels and against the right edge: a dim M while nothing is stored, the value beside it once something is. It was a line at the top of the history panel, where it could only be read with that panel open

Every on/off setting is one block at the top of the settings panel, each on its own line with the switch against the right edge. Two of them are new: Save window size, and Save history, which keeps the history list in config.toml and reads it back on the next start, updated as each calculation lands
Theme is a row of buttons like every other choice in the panel rather than a drop-down, and it and the font list go last, since they are the two longest controls and the two you set once
The settings panel carries the version in its bottom-right corner, and the window's minimum width can be pinned with min_window_width in config.toml for a small screen or a tiling desktop
The readout is bigger again: it keeps about a seventh of its line as leading rather than three tenths, split evenly above and below the digits
¹⁄ₓ and ⁺⁄₋ are drawn as the fractions they are, numerator over denominator, rather than three characters in a row

x² and x³ finish the operation. The exponent they write is not a slot anything keyed next can reach, so 5, x², 3 is 5²×3 with the multiplication filled in — it used to run onto the end of the exponent and give 5 to the twenty-third. Nothing postfix reaches in either: 5² then ! is (5²)! and then xʸ is (5²)^y, since a bare 5^2! reads as 5 raised to 2!
A factorial keyed in a caret's exponent still belongs there: 2, xʸ, 3, ! is 2 raised to 3!, which is the reading both power keys are reached for

x² and x³ square the number on screen rather than the piece of it the cursor is parked in front of. 6, yˣ, 3 reads 3⁶ with the cursor still in the base slot, and x² there is now (3⁶)² where it wrote 3^2^6 — the 3 raised to the sixty-fourth

Backspace and C part company over a fixed exponent, because they ask different questions. Backspace takes back the press, so 5² gives the 5 back; C takes back the value, and 5² is one value, so 5+2³ then C is 5+

% never lands in an exponent. It is a basic-keypad operation on the value in hand and the text cannot say otherwise — 2^5% reads as 2 raised to 5% — so the press leaves the exponent and brackets the power: (2⁵)%. Open a bracket at the head of the exponent and it stays there, since that gesture is for putting a whole expression in the slot

The brackets a script slot shows stay up once you have typed into it, drawn round what is there rather than in place of it, for as long as the cursor is still in the slot: 2⁽¹⁵⁾ while the exponent is being keyed, with the opener lit and the closer dim. One digit does not mean you are finished with a number, and nothing else on screen said the next one lands up there too. A slot you opened a bracket of your own at the head of, or filled with a call, wears no second pair

logᵧ and ʸ√x fill in one order whatever is on screen when you reach them: the argument or the radicand first, then the base or the degree. 0.1.7 read the empty display the other way round, which made the keys do one thing on a fresh display and another on a typed one. logᵧ, 8, ), 2 reads log₂(8), and ʸ√x, 8, ), 3 reads ³√(8)

Backspace unwinds one of those calls in that same order reversed, last piece first: into the base or the degree, out through its characters, back inside the brackets to the argument, out through its characters, and only with both slots empty does the call itself come off
The degree of a root sits half a character into the radical rather than a whole one, which had pushed it past the opening and onto the stroke

The square and cube root keys wear the whole operation — ²√x and ³√x, the way ʸ√x does with its degree left open — rather than a bare sign that says which radical it is but not what it does to what is on screen
1⁄x and +⁄− use the fraction slash the percent sign is built from, which leans further over than the ASCII one and so reads as a division rather than as a separator

The readout is bigger. It was giving up about three tenths of its line to leading, and the gaps around the display were the keypad's inter-row spacing stacked either side of it; both are smaller now, and the digits scale into the room that gives back

logᵧ and ʸ√x opened from an empty display ask for the base and the degree first — the part the key was reached for — and ) moves in to the argument: logᵧ, 2, ), 8 reads log₂(8), and ʸ√x, 3, ), 8 reads ³√(8). With an operand already typed nothing changes

Backspace unwinds one of those calls the way it was filled: through the argument, back into the slot beside it, and only then the call itself. Neither argument can be deleted out from under the call any more, so log₇₁(98) cannot quietly become log(7198) and ³√(8) cannot become √(83) — and a call with anything typed in it is never taken off in a single press

The font you picked is in force from the first frame. The desktop's own toolkit settings arrive a moment after launch and used to overwrite it, leaving the keypad and the panels in the system font until a family was picked by hand

The keys draw their own superscripts and subscripts rather than asking the font for a raised or lowered glyph it may not carry. The y under logᵧ, the x of 2ˣ and the degrees of ³√ and ʸ√x were each drawn by whichever face happened to have them, at whatever height that face put them; now every script on the keypad is the key's own typeface at one height

) with nothing open to close brackets the whole power rather than the exponent that ends it: 2^3 then ) is (2^3), ready to be squared or divided into, instead of 2⁽³⁾ — the same value with brackets round a part of it nobody asked to separate

An operator keyed while the cursor is still in the base slot yˣ opens goes after the whole power: 2, yˣ, 3, + reads 3²+. It used to land between the base and the caret, leaving a power with no base and the operand out of the sum
A root degree that is itself a root sits in its own radical. Second- and third-level degrees were drawn a character to the left of the sign they belong to
Opening a side panel no longer flashes a rescaled window: the panel waits for the width it is going to stand in, and the calculator column holds its own width while the window grows around it
History, mode and settings wear the button shape you configured, like every other button in the window
The "Show ASCII expression" toggle loses the example line under it

Every root wears the same radical, the cube root included: ³√(8) rather than the single ∛ glyph that a good many fonts do not carry and draw as a box. The key face matches, and the expression is still cbrt(8) wherever it is written down
Backspace and C never leave the calculator's own work on screen. A × it inserted for you goes when the operand it multiplied goes, so backspacing the (2) out of 5×(2) leaves 5 rather than 5×

What one press wrote, one press takes back: x² on 2^2 writes (2^2)², and one backspace gives back the 2^2 rather than an empty exponent slot. An exponent you have since typed into is yours, and comes apart a character at a time again

Backspace retraces a cursor the keypad moved. yˣ parks it in front of what you typed and logᵧ / ʸ√x park it in a slot; in each case backspace takes that press back and returns the cursor to where the press found it. yˣ used to stick there with nothing to its left to delete, and ʸ√x left a root missing an argument
x² and x³ square and cube what is on screen instead of adding a level to it: 2^3 then x² is (2^3)² = 64, where a second caret would have said 2^3^2 = 512. xʸ is still the key for building a tower
yˣ counts the whole power it would raise rather than the operand under the cursor, so it stops at three levels like every other key: pressed on the 4 of 4^3^2 it is refused instead of making a fourth
) with nothing open to close brackets the operand you just typed — 5+2 then ) reads 5+(2) — instead of doing nothing
The degree of a root sits in the opening of the radical rather than beside it

Three levels of script is as deep as an expression goes, so what is on screen stays readable: 2^2^2 is drawn in full, and a key that would write a fourth puts what is there in brackets and starts again from the line — x² on 2^2^2 gives (2^2^2)². logᵧ and ʸ√x need no added brackets, since a call carries its own: logᵧ on 2^2^8 reads log₍₎(2^2^8)

The caption above the display is drawn as the same sized pieces as the display itself, so an expression reads the same in both. A single line of one size could only raise the first level and fell back to brackets after it, turning 2^2^2 into 2⁽2²⁾

"Show ASCII expression" shows exactly what Copy would put on the clipboard, character for character: pi, e, sqrt(, * and / rather than the pretty letters, the radical and the display's own digit grouping
What Copy puts on the clipboard is now plain ASCII throughout — Euler's number goes out as e, with the multiplication spelled out where a bare e would read as scientific notation (2*e3)
The degree of a root is written into the radical rather than beside it, half a character to the right, the way ⁴√ is printed as one symbol
yˣ shows the empty base slot in front of the operand it raised, dim while the cursor is in it, so it is clear the next digit goes under what is already there
xʸ needs a base and no longer invents one: on an empty display — where the 0 on screen is the calculator's, not yours — the press does nothing, as yˣ already did

Exponents and bases are drawn as ordinary text at a smaller size, moved off the line, rather than swapped for Unicode's raised glyphs — so anything can go up: a decimal separator (2¹·⁵ in either locale), a factorial, or a whole call. Press xʸ then sin and the call goes up as a call, and a power inside a power steps up again

ʸ√x writes its degree in front of the radical, ⁴√(16) rather than √(16,4), and the degree can now be reached from an empty display: ʸ√x, 8, ), 3 is the cube root of 8, the same gesture logᵧ uses for its base. Until now the degree could only be typed by entering the radicand first

C takes back the last operand — the number, the bracketed group or the whole function call you just finished — and leaves the expression it was part of standing. With an operator under the cursor there is nothing to take back, so the press only flips the key to AC, which clears the display
The closing bracket of a logᵧ goes back to the active colour once the cursor drops to the base, instead of staying dim as though the operand were still open
A slot you have opened but not filled — an exponent, a logᵧ base, a root degree — draws its small brackets dimmed while the cursor is in them, so it is clear where the next digit lands
Arithmetic is done in base ten, so the numbers you type are the numbers that get added: 0.1 + 0.2 − 0.3 is 0 and 0.3 mod 0.1 is 0, where binary answered 5.55e-17 and a clean-looking, wrong 0.1
A result carried into the next calculation keeps the precision it was computed at rather than the fifteen digits it was shown to, so 1÷3 = ×3 = gives back 1
A first run opens on the Basic keypad; Scientific is one press of the top bar away, and whichever you leave it on is the one it opens on next time
The window size is remembered, written out a couple of seconds after you stop dragging rather than on every frame of the drag
With a side panel open the window can no longer be dragged in narrower than the calculator plus the panel, which used to leave the keypad with nothing
Opening or closing a side panel no longer flashes a frame of shifted buttons
A fractional exponent stays raised — 2¹·⁵ rather than 2⁽1.5⁾ — in whichever decimal separator is in use
logᵧ writes its base under the log, and shows the empty slot until you type one: log₍₎(8) becomes log₂(8)
The Scientific keypad fills all nine columns, and 2nd is left to the ten keys that genuinely have an inverse — π, xʸ, ʸ√x and √ now hold still under your fingers
New yˣ key: the same two operands as xʸ read the other way round, so 2, yˣ, 3 is 9 where 2, xʸ, 3 is 8
The caret is off the display — exponents are raised outright (2⁵), and one Unicode cannot raise is written at full size inside raised brackets (2⁽2!⁾)
ʸ√x and logᵧ close the argument they wrapped, so the second one can be reached at all, and root(16,4) wears the radical as √(16,4)
Power keys hold still where there is no operand, instead of taking a base you never typed
Opening a side panel no longer leaves the window scaled and blurry with the pointer landing on the wrong button
The settings panel opens without its first-time freeze: the font caches are warmed on a background thread
Panel scrollbars sit beside the rows they scroll rather than over them, and the separator and button-shape choices are visible rows of buttons rather than drop-downs
The keypad layout is now configurable: every cell of both keypads, and what the 2nd key toggles, is set in config.toml
One % key covers both percentage and modulo, decided by what follows it
Button labels are centred on their ink, so they no longer drift with the chosen font
The 2nd key is visibly lit while it is armed
Number properties are shown in the basic layout too
